question.text: Mr. Suresh Kumar, a shareholder in 'Lotus MediTech', wishes to dispose of his shares. The Category II AIF 'Vindhya Capital' holds a Right of First Refusal (ROFR). Under a ROFR (as distinct from ROFO):

answer.text: The AIF must first offer a price, then the selling shareholder can seek a better market offer
The selling shareholder may sell freely but must inform the AIF within 30 days post-sale
The AIF automatically acquires the shares at book value without any market-quote process
The selling shareholder must first obtain the best market quote and then offer the shares to the AIF at that matched quote, which the AIF may accept or refuse

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Ch 11.6.6 (Exit Rights), under ROFR, the selling shareholder must approach the ROFR-holder WITH THE BEST QUOTE FROM MARKET PARTICIPANTS. The ROFR-holder then chooses to buy by matching that best quote, or refuses. This is OPPOSITE to ROFO, where the ROFO-holder offers first. The Trap: Option A describes ROFO, not ROFR. Option C invents a book-value mechanism. Option D defeats the pre-emptive purpose of ROFR. Cross-Exam Context: ROFR/ROFO distinction is a favourite XIX-A and XIX-C MCQ — always verify which side offers first. Manager's Pro-Tip: ROFR is better for the holder when the market is hot (more bidders = more competitive price). ROFO is better when the market is cold (fewer bidders = lower baseline). Negotiate based on expected exit conditions.
